content: {"id": "8ca59e5b-05dd-4852-b2f3-fa3e727df3b4", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Connections to 10.0.4.40:8080 immediately fail with 'connection refused' and tshark shows RST,ACK coming back from 10.0.4.40. Should I open the security group?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "2750e15c-afa4-4bb6-817e-2d3951842d51", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "No, a security group change won't fix this — the packet pattern you're describing is actually telling you the opposite.

Here's why: when a security group blocks traffic, the packet is silently dropped at the VPC level — the client just sees a timeout, with no response at all from the remote host. What you're seeing (`RST,ACK` coming back from `10.0.4.40` itself) means the SYN **made it through** the network and security group just fine, and the host at `10.0.4.40` actively rejected the connection at the TCP level.

A RST,ACK on connect almost always means one of:
- **Nothing is listening on port 8080** on that host (most common cause — process not started, crashed, or bound to a different port/interface)
- A host-based firewall (iptables/nftables/firewalld) on `10.0.4.40` is explicitly rejecting (not dropping) traffic to that port
- The service is bound to `127.0.0.1` only, not the `10.0.4.40` interface, so external connections get refused

Opening the security group wider will have no effect since the SG isn't in the path of the problem.

If you want, I can check whether there's a listener on port 8080 on that instance and look at its recent activity — happy to dig into that if you give me the instance ID or let me look it up by IP.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
